items.title: Film Quote of the Day: The Robert De Niro Line From 1987 That May Be His Most Underrated
items.summary: Robert De Niro is one of those actors that I just buy in any role. So when he played Satan in a 1987 film noir, I was all in. Angel Heart is a psychological thriller that I feel like barely gets talked about today. It recently got a 4K restoration that's pristine, and I want to encourage everyone to actually go check it out. There's some epic Mickey Rourke moment in the movie, and seeing these guys play off one another is special. There's one line De Niro has in the movie that is a big reveal and lines up the plot in perfect noir-speak. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The Scene in Question Alan Parker’s Angel Heart is a wild hybrid of a 1940s detective mystery and supernatural horror, all rolled up into a kind of sexy mystery. You get Mickey Rourke playing Harry Angel, a down-on-his-luck Brooklyn P.I. hired by a mysterious, impeccably dressed client with long fingernails and a well-groomed beard named Louis Cyphre (say that name out loud slowly if you haven't seen it). It's at this moment I pause to say this whole idea rocks, and the movie knows it, leaning into the batshit moments and letting you have fun and get scared with them, too. Cyphre wants Angel to track down a missing singer named Johnny Favorite, and he can pay well for the job. So it gets taken. De Niro plays Satan with panache, blending into the background and hanging with everyday people so you see him pop up in a Harlem church, in a diner eating hard-boiled eggs, and all over the city. During one of their meetings, as Harry gets closer to unraveling a truth he really shouldn't be digging into, Cyphre drops some evil wisdom on him. "However cleverly you sneak up on a mirror, your reflection always looks you straight in the eye." - YouTubewww.youtube.com What The Quote Means On a purely cinematic level, it’s a brilliant piece of writing that was adapted from William Hjortsberg’s novel Falling Angel. items.title: The 10 Westerns Every Filmmaker Should Watch
items.summary: Western movies have been embraced for almost a century because they take us back to a lawless time that I think carries a lot of aspirational qualities for many Americans. But today, I want to nerd out on something Westerns do that I think makes filmmakers swoon. I find this genre to be the ultimate conduit for visual storytelling. Since the genre is so malleable, we not only get those epic shots but also the intimate ones and everything in between. Here are 10 Westerns every filmmaker needs to study, along with some lessons you can take from each title. Let's dive in. 1. The Searchers (1956) - YouTube www.youtube.com Director: John Ford Writer: Frank S. Nugent (based on the novel by Alan Le May) Cast: John Wayne, Jeffrey Hunter, Vera Miles, Ward Bond, Natalie Wood Cinematographer: Winton C. Hoch Why Study This Movie? No one shoots a movie like John Ford. Just ask a young Steven Spielberg, who met him and learned about horizon lines from him. This is one of the greatest movies in history. There's this sulking beauty underneath it all. An anger from John Wayne that is palpable. Also, it's a masterclass in framing, depth of field, and character geography. Study how Ford creates isolation through framing within framing. Those iconic shots of Wayne in the open and Wayne in the doorway bookended the story. 2. High Noon (1952) - YouTube www.youtube.com Director: Fred Zinnemann Writer: Carl Foreman Cast: Gary Cooper, Grace Kelly, Thomas Mitchell, Lloyd Bridges, Katy Jurado Cinematographer: Floyd Crosby Why Study This Movie? Have you ever heard of a time lock in screenwriting? This is a pressure cooker. And High Noon is the gold standard for real-time pacing. The whole movie is 85 minutes, so from the opening shot to the closing, we get a natural unfolding of the tale. For a wrtierl ike me, this is catnip. And directors lean in, too. items.title: 10 Essential Movies of 1995 Every Film Fan Should See
items.summary: The 1990s were an exciting time for cinephiles, with rising filmmakers like Quentin Tarantino, John Singleton, The Wachowskis, Sofia Coppola, Robert Rodriguez, and Kevin Smith churning out their first masterpieces, independent cinema stepping out into the spotlight in a major way, horror reinventing itself multiple times, and much more. There was so much going on in the 1990s that it can be hard to keep track of what to watch, so let’s simplify things by drilling down on 10 essential titles from one single year out of that entire decade: 1995. 10. Se7en Another legendary filmmaker who had their feature directorial debut in the 1990s was David Fincher. Long before Fight Club or The Social Network or Gone Girl came his sophomore feature, Se7en. Although his actual debut, 1992’s Alien 3, ended up being a compromised effort, the serial killer thriller Se7en perfectly captures the technically precise, but often edgy and squalid sensibility that he would bring to his future work. 9. Sense and Sensibility The success of the Jane Austen adaptation Sense and Sensibility, which was a financial smash hit in addition to being nominated for seven Oscars (winning one) and six Golden Globes (winning two), has had a huge ripple effect. First of all, as Ang Lee’s first full English-language feature, it led the filmmaker to become a huge success in the United States, allowing him to keep working in the language, helming other huge titles like Brokeback Mountain and Life of Pi. However, as part of the Jane Austen Renaissance of 1995, which included the Colin Firth Pride and Prejudice miniseries and the Emma adaptation Clueless (more on that later), it also led to a resurgence of interest in Jane Austen’s work that has resulted in a flood of major adaptations of the literary giant’s work (including everything from 2005’s Pride and Prejudice to Bridget Jones’s Diary to Becoming Jane to Fire Island). 8. items.title: The 3 "Laws of Hollywood" Every Filmmaker Should Know
items.summary: People are always trying to crack the code of how to make it in the entertainment industry. And it's true, it's a world that does seem to operate under an invisible framework you only come to understand when you're in it, and you learn the hierarchies of managers and executives and assistants and mailrooms. Every once in a while, someone tries to parse the industry's intricate ceremonies. Enter Peter M. Hoffman, a unique voice in indie film who recently spoke to Film Courage about his career and viewpoint. Hoffman became President and CEO of Carolco Pictures (the independent studio founded by Mario Kassar and Andrew Vajna that produced Terminator 2: Judgment Day, Basic Instinct, Total Recall, and Rambo III) during its late-'80s and early-'90s peak. He founded Seven Arts Entertainment in 1992 and produced The Believer, Johnny Mnemonic, Stander, Asylum, and Rules of Engagement. In 2015, Hoffman was convicted on federal wire fraud charges in a Louisiana film-tax-credit case, a conviction he continues to dispute. He wrote his memoir Karmic Winds during his prison sentence. In this video, he names his three laws of Hollywood and how to work under them. Let's learn more together. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Three Laws of Hollywood "The first law in Hollywood is that no good deed goes unpunished." He doesn't elaborate. But does he need to? There are too many finicky personalities on a set for you to perform perfectly every single time. He's joking here, but there's a bittersweet truth to it too. "And the second law in Hollywood that I like to say is that it's not enough that I succeed. My friends have to fail. There's a certain sanguine quality to the competitiveness in our business. Sometimes we don't give the recognition to our colleagues' success that perhaps we should, and therefore some of the cattiness that you see comes out of that."
